humanities_role_explanation: SimpleQA is a general short-form factuality benchmark. Topics such as history (n=173), art (n=550) and music (n=341) only supply trivia-style items. The competence tested is factual accuracy and calibration, not humanistic interpretation or disciplinary skill.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Text-only short questions with short text answers.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Short, fact-seeking questions with a single indisputable answer (dates, persons, numbers, places), graded as correct, incorrect or not attempted. Calibration is measured through stated confidence and answer frequency over 100 samples. No interpretive work is required.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Broad multi-topic factuality benchmark (science & technology, politics, art, geography, sports, music, TV, history, video games), but scoped to short-form factual QA.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Claude-3 haiku, sonnet and opus, Claude-3.5-sonnet, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o1-mini and o1-preview.

quantitative_metrics.note: Correct, not attempted, incorrect, correct given attempted, F-score; calibration plots.

summary: SimpleQA is an adversarially collected benchmark of 4,326 short fact-seeking questions with single, indisputable answers, built against GPT-4 responses. It grades answers as correct, incorrect or not attempted, and also measures model calibration. Frontier models score under 50%.
key_findings: o1-preview scores highest (42.7 correct, F-score 44.8), followed by GPT-4o (38.2). Claude models attempt fewer questions. Larger models are better calibrated, but all models overstate their confidence. The estimated benchmark error rate is about 3%.
facets_explanation: Questions and reference answers were written by 'AI trainers' (human annotators), verified by a second independent trainer, and kept only if the two answers matched. Each answer required sources from two distinct web domains. The paper does not describe the trainers as trained in any humanities discipline, so 'domain_expert' is a weak fit and 'crowd_annotation' is a plausible alternative; it is used here because the trainers were hired annotators who followed a detailed protocol with dual verification, though the paper does not state that they held disciplinary training. Questions with disagreement, ambiguity or multiple answers were removed. The questions are closed-book, so the answer is not in the stimulus.
results_explanation: Table 3 reports 'OpenAI o1-preview 42.7 9.2 48.1 47.0 44.8', i.e. correct 42.7, not attempted 9.2, incorrect 48.1, correct given attempted 47.0, F-score 44.8. The headline score is the 'Correct' column for o1-preview. A third trainer scored 94.4% on 1,000 sampled items, but this is a data-quality check and not a comparable human baseline on the model metric, so no gap is computed.
